Find ${lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted above.
questions.worked_solution:
From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=3.$ 

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5}={lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,1}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x))}^{3} \\  & =(3-1)^{3} \\  & ={2}^{3} \\  & =8,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{4} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,1}(f(x)-4{x}^{2}))}^{5} \\  & =(3-4(1)^{2})^{5} \\  & =(-1)^{5} \\  & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5} & ={lim}_{x\to \,1}(3-x)^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,1}(f(x)-4{x}^{2})^{5} \\  & =8\cdot (-1) \\  & =-8\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to 3}{(\frac{4f(x)-12}{{x}^{2}-2x+2})}^{2}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted above.
questions.worked_solution:
Using the power and quotient rules, we can rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}{(\frac{4f(x)-12}{{x}^{2}-2x+2})}^{2} & ={(\frac{{lim}_{x\to 3}(4f(x)-12)}{{lim}_{x\to 3}({x}^{2}-2x+2)})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The above is true provided that  ${lim}_{x\to 3}f(x)$ exists.

We find from the graph that ${lim}_{x\to 3}f(x)=4.$ We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

$$
{lim}_{x\to 3}(4f(x)-12)=4(4)-12=4
$$

and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 3}({x}^{2}-2x+2)={3}^{2}-2(3)+2=5
$$

So we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}{(\frac{4f(x)-12}{{x}^{2}-2x+2})}^{2} & ={(\frac{{lim}_{x\to 3}(4f(x)-12)}{{lim}_{x\to 3}({x}^{2}-2x+2)})}^{2} \\  & ={(\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{16}{25}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Applying the Power Rule to Compute a Limit
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Here, we apply the product rule and the power rule to get

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}\left[(2x-1)^3(x-2)^9\right]   &= \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(2x-1)^3\cdot  \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(x-2)^9\[3pt]
                                                                                    &= \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(2x-1)\right)^3\cdot  \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 3}(x-2)\right)^9\[3pt]
                                                                                    &= (2\cdot 3 -1)^3\cdot (3-2)^9\[3pt]
                                                                                    &= 5^3 \cdot 1^9\[3pt]
                                                                                    & = 125.
}
$$

Example: 
                    Applying the Power Rule to Compute a Limit Given a Graph
canonical_examples.problem:
The figure below shows the graph of $f(x).$ Determine $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} \left(\dfrac{2-7x}{xf(x)+2}\right)^3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198442/assets/5059a2cee34ad8547bf1af6239ab4a8356e715cd920707cf5f33d2de105a5c1d.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the graph, we find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} f(x)=3.$ Therefore, using the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}{(\frac{2-7x}{xf(x)+2})}^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{2-7x}{xf(x)+2})}^{3} \\  & ={(\frac{2-7(2)}{(2\cdot 3)+2})}^{3} \\  & ={(\frac{-12}{8})}^{3} \\  & ={(\frac{-3}{2})}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{27}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying the Root Rule to Compute a Limit
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1} \dfrac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2}
=\dfrac{\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1} \sqrt{x+8}}{\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}(x-2)}.
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

Applying the root rule in the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\sqrt{x+8} & =\sqrt{{lim}_{x\to 1}(x+8)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+8} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

For the denominator, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}(x-2) & =1-2 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\sqrt{x+8}}{x-2} & =\frac{3}{(-1)} \\  & =-3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow -2}\left(\dfrac{f(x)}{x^2-1}\right)^{2/3}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14198442/assets/583e67513466b35aafcae69c81d5703b45ffada4bdc08bb34de15ee6ce1d53e5.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to the power rule and the quotient rules,

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}{(\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}-1})}^{2/3} & ={(\frac{{lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)}{{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}-1)})}^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We find from the graph that the limit of the numerator is

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow -2} f(x)=1.
$$

 We also calculate the limit of the denominator as
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}-1) & =(-2)^{2}-1=3.\end{aligned}
$$

 So we get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}{(\frac{f(x)}{{x}^{2}-1})}^{2/3} & ={(\frac{{lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)}{{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}-1)})}^{2/3} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{9}}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **power rule** states that the limit of a power is the power of the limit. More precisely, if $n$ is any positive integer and $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to a}(f(x))^{n}={({lim}_{x\to a}f(x))}^{n}={L}^{n}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, with the power rule, we can evaluate a limit like 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}(3x-4)^{8}
$$

 by evaluating the limit of the expression within parentheses and then taking the power of the result.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-4)^{8} & ={({lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-4))}^{8} \\  & =(3\cdot 2-4)^{8} \\  & ={2}^{8} \\  & =256\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to a}(f(x))^{n}={({lim}_{x\to a}f(x))}^{n}={L}^{n}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, with the power rule, we can evaluate a limit like 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}(3x-4)^{8}
$$

 by evaluating the limit of the expression within parentheses and then taking the power of the result.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-4)^{8} & ={({lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-4))}^{8} \\  & =(3\cdot 2-4)^{8} \\  & ={2}^{8} \\  & =256\,.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: The Root Rule for Limits
tutorials.problem:
The **root rule** states that the limit of a root is the root of the limit (provided that the root exists).

More precisely, if $n$ is any positive integer and $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to a}\sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{{lim}_{x\to a}f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, with the root rule, we can evaluate a limit like 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}\sqrt{3x-2}
$$

 by evaluating the limit of the expression within the root and then taking the root of the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt{3x-2} & =\sqrt{{lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-2)} \\  & =\sqrt{3\cdot 2-2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: The Root Rule for Limits
tutorials.content:
The **root rule** states that the limit of a root is the root of the limit (provided that the root exists).

More precisely, if $n$ is any positive integer and $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to a}\sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{{lim}_{x\to a}f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, with the root rule, we can evaluate a limit like 

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}\sqrt{3x-2}
$$

 by evaluating the limit of the expression within the root and then taking the root of the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt{3x-2} & =\sqrt{{lim}_{x\to 2}(3x-2)} \\  & =\sqrt{3\cdot 2-2} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Combining Different Rules
tutorials.problem:
If we combine the power rule and the root rule, then we get the following useful generalization: if $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}f(x)=L,$ then for any fraction $p/q,$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a}\left(f(x)\right)^{p/q} =  \left(\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow a} f(x)\right)^{p/q} = L^{p/q}
$$

provided that $L^{p/q}$ exists.

For example, we can evaluate a limit like 

$$
\lim_\limits{y\rightarrow 64} y^{-1/6}
$$

 by evaluating the limit of $y$ and then exponentiating the result to the fractional exponent:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{y\to 64}{y}^{-1/6} & ={({lim}_{y\to 64}y)}^{-1/6} \\  & =(64)^{-1/6} \\  & ={({2}^{6})}^{-1/6} \\  & ={2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
